title: The history of the car industry

paragraphs.text: The growth of the car has been an extraordinary story, as remarkable for its destructive powers as its benefits. In London, at the beginning of the 20th century, horses were the primary transport, and speeds across the city were faster than they are today in a car. Yet horses were an expensive luxury, so for the most part people simply did not travel far. By the end of that century, the world’s car makers were employing nearly four million people to produce 35,801,618 cars in a single year, to add to the estimated 500 million in daily use around the globe.

In the 13th century, Roger Bacon mentioned the possibility of carriages propelled without the use of animals, and in the 15th century, in Italy, Leonardo da Vinci sketched a self-moving car. But the first record of a powered vehicle comes from the Astronomia Europea, published in 1687. The small carriage was fuelled with a pan of hot coals. Steam generated by the heat of the coals turned a simple turbine, which was geared to the front axle of the vehicle. The carriage was constructed under the supervision of Father Ferdinand Verbiest, a missionary who spent a large part of his life in China, and was appointed Astronomer Royal to Emperor Kang-Hsi.

The motor car’s time came in the 19th century with the emergence of unstable fuels such as coal gas and liquid petroleum spirit. In 1829, Samuel Brown of London produced a vehicle powered by a four-horsepower, gas-vacuum engine. This was a true three-stroke*, internal-combustion engine, which in trials managed to climb the notoriously steep Shooters Hill on the outskirts of the city, but it was wildly uneconomical compared with contemporary steam engines, and little came of it.

In 1862, the French engineer Alphonse Beau de Rochas proposed a four-stroke explosion cycle, the basis on which almost all modern car engines operate. Rochas patented his engine design, but did not build it. His paper coincided with the work of Nikolaus August Otto, who had been developing the first commercially available gas engine. In 1862, Otto prepared a gas-powered engine that operated on the four-stroke cycle proposed by Rochas, but it promptly blew to pieces. Otto was then joined by Gottlieb Daimler, the son of a German baker, who patented a high-speed petrol engine in 1876. At the same time, in Mannheim, Karl Benz started working on a petrol tricycle. This 3-wheeled vehicle took to the streets in 1885, was patented the following year, and offered for sale in 1887. Benz granted an agency to Emile Roger in Paris, and the modern motor industry was born.

In August 1888, Bertha Benz borrowed her husband’s car without permission. She packed provisions and her two young sons on board and drove off to visit relatives in Pforzheim, some 75 miles from Mannheim. On the way, Bertha had to fill up with dry-cleaning fluid when she ran out of fuel; she repaired an electrical circuit with clothing elastic, unblocked a fuel line with a hat pin, and found a shoe mender to re-line a brake. She arrived safely, and five days later she drove home again; it was the first ever long-distance journey by motor car.

Another woman played a major role in the creation of the first recognizably modern motor car, the 1894 Panhard-Levassor. In 1890, Louise Sarazin had succeeded in selling Gottlieb Daimler’s engine and mechanical patents to a company in France after the death of her husband, who had initiated the deal. The Panhard-Levassor company used Daimler’s engine to construct the first modern motor car. It had an improved layout, consisting of an enclosed, front-mounted, twin-cylinder engine, attached gearbox, and foot-operated clutch. This was the first successful move away from the way parts had been arranged in previous vehicles.

In the early years, cars developed more rapidly than computers in today's IT industry. In 1894, motor cars were no faster than a horse; ten years later they were commonly capable of 80 miles per hour and some had achieved a speed of over 100 miles per hour. Making cars soon became a study in productivity, with Henry Ford leading the way. In 1914, Ford designed a production line which moved along continuously. His claim that ‘any customer can have any colour he wants so long as it’s black’ was startlingly honest: his methods manufactured cars so quickly that this was the only colour of paint that would dry fast enough.

Since the 1970s, companies such as Volkswagen and Toyota have dominated car making. The VW Beetle became the world’s most popular car by combining reliability with charm. In January 1978, the last German-built VW Beetle rolled off the lines, but production continued overseas. In May 1981, the 20 millionth Beetle was completed in Mexico, where the car was nicknamed the belly button – because everyone had one.

In the 1970s, legislation introduced to protect the environment and enhance safety raised the price of entry into car production, and gradually car makers fell by the wayside. Even those old names that remain, such as Jaguar, Aston Martin, Alfa Romeo, Lancia, Volvo and Ferrari, are part of much bigger groups, which themselves are being taken over by even bigger car-making combines.

The 1980s and the 1990s witnessed a battle for world domination among car makers, and a fight to keep costs down. In the present day, the industry spends its time building as many different cars as possible on the same frame, and exporting production to economies where wages are considerably lower.
